final_recommendation: The room converged on a binding enforcement protocol (separate from the base USMCA) with automatic tariff suspension if Mexico fails to resolve wage violations within 60 days. Mexico commits to signing by mid-December; Congress commits to a January 15 vote contingent on bulletproof tariff-trigger language in Friday's draft. Canada insists the base agreement remains locked (November 30 signing) and will not reopen.
minority_objections: Canada repeatedly insisted the base USMCA (November 30 signing) must not be reopened, treating the protocol as strictly separate
Mexico held a sovereignty red line: Mexican inspectors must lead enforcement, with U.S. observers only—no unilateral U.S. inspection authority
key_conflicts: Congress vs. Mexico on enforcement sovereignty: Congress demanded U.S. inspection rights; Mexico insisted Mexican inspectors lead with U.S. observers only
Timeline pressure: Business lobby demanded January 15 vote; Congress and labor refused to commit until Friday's draft text proved bulletproof
Definition of 'resolved': Mexico wanted flexibility on corrective action plans; Congress/labor demanded demonstrable wage adjustment on the books
key_concessions: Mexico accepted 3-facility threshold and automatic tariff suspension on day 61 (no waiver discretion)
Congress accepted Mexican-led enforcement with U.S. observers (not unilateral U.S. inspection)
Trade lawyer locked 'resolved' to mean demonstrable wage adjustment, not filed plans
Mexico committed to 5-day remediation order issuance timeline to prevent dispute delays
red_lines: Congress/labor: automatic tariff suspension with zero waiver discretion or investigation loopholes
Mexico: Mexican inspectors must lead enforcement; no unilateral U.S. authority on Mexican soil
Canada: base USMCA (November 30 signing) will not be reopened; protocol is strictly separate
Labor: tariff trigger must say 'automatic suspension on day 61' with no wiggle room on 'resolved'
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Implementation risk: no discussion of how Mexican inspectors will be trained, funded, or held accountable for enforcement quality
Political risk in Mexico: no discussion of how Mexico's government will sell binding U.S. tariff authority to its own legislature
Dispute resolution: minimal discussion of what happens if the U.S. and Mexico disagree on whether a violation is 'resolved'
Timeline slippage: Friday draft deadline is aggressive; no contingency if trade lawyer misses it or if labor/Congress find gaps over the weekend
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Friday's draft text actually contains bulletproof tariff-trigger language with zero loopholes
Whether labor's weekend review surfaces new enforcement gaps requiring Tuesday-Wednesday rewrites
Whether Mexico's legislature ratifies a protocol giving the U.S. automatic tariff authority over Mexican labor compliance
Whether Canada's insistence on keeping the base agreement locked holds if protocol negotiations drag into January
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved conditional convergence on a protocol structure, but ratification depends entirely on Friday's draft text being bulletproof. Labor explicitly refused to endorse until they vet the text over the weekend. If gaps emerge, the timeline collapses (mid-December signing becomes uncertain, January 15 vote at risk). Mexico's domestic ratification of the protocol remains unaddressed. Canada's red line (no base agreement reopening) creates a hard boundary but also a fallback: if the protocol stalls, Canada ratifies the base deal without it.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress opened with 'it doesn't pass as drafted' and threatened to walk; the entire meeting was driven by the need to amend the package to secure votes
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor demanded binding facility inspections, automatic tariff triggers, and bulletproof language with zero loopholes—drove every round of negotiation
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business lobby pushed hard for timeline certainty (January 15 vote) and threatened capital holds, but did not dominate the room's direction—labor enforcement did
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly insisted the base agreement (including dairy) stays locked and will not reopen, but this was defensive positioning, not a driving theme
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's red line on inspector-led enforcement (not U.S. unilateral authority) shaped every compromise on the protocol structure
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media actor pushed for clean headline language and public narrative, but was secondary to the substantive enforcement negotiations
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: The room treated the base agreement as unstable without a binding protocol—Congress threatened to reopen, Canada insisted on separation, Mexico committed to signing by mid-December to avoid collapse
